opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when I first moved into AI, there was definitely a period where it felt like my progress slowed down a lot. My earlier work was much closer to formal methods and programming languages, where I had built up intuition over years. I knew which problems were important, which directions were likely to work, and how to judge my own results. When I switched, a lot of that intuition didn't transfer directly, so for a while I was basically a beginner again: reading papers, running experiments that didn't go anywhere, and not producing much that I felt proud of.

At the time, it was stressful. In a PhD, everyone is quietly counting papers, and you see peers moving fast while you feel stuck. But looking back, I understand that gap differently. It wasn't wasted time; it was the cost of building a new foundation. You can't skip the stage where you learn the field's language, its benchmarks, its engineering realities, and what people actually care about.

And interestingly, my background did come back to help, just not in the way I expected. The habit of thinking about systems rigorously, about abstractions, about how to design something clean and general, turned out to be very useful when I started working on LLM serving and systems, things like how to make inference efficient and programmable. Some of the ideas that worked best came precisely from looking at AI problems with a systems and PL mindset.

So my takeaway is: a gap in output during a transition is normal, and it's often a sign that you're actually learning something new rather than repeating what you already know. The key is to keep building, stay close to people who are strong in the new area, and trust that the depth you had before will eventually connect with the new field. When it does, that combination can become your real advantage.

r001.rationale: The response describes a general slowdown while transitioning into AI. It does not say outsiders attributed her research output to a full year of work or that she produced it in the final three months.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I felt that gap very acutely. My background was in theoretical computer science and databases, so when I moved into AI, especially large language model systems, there was this period where it seemed like everyone around me already spoke a language I was still learning. People were publishing papers on topics I had barely read about, and the field was moving so fast that by the time I understood one idea, three more had come out.

What helped me was reframing what the gap actually was. I thought of it as a knowledge gap, like I was behind on reading. But really it was more of an orientation gap. I didn't yet know which problems mattered, which results were real versus hype, and where my own skills could actually contribute. Once I saw it that way, I stopped trying to catch up on everything and started looking for places where my systems and database background was an advantage rather than a liability.

That turned out to be serving and inference. Running these models efficiently is fundamentally a systems problem, with scheduling, memory management, and caching. Those were things I already knew how to think about. So the gap closed not because I became an expert in every part of deep learning, but because I found an intersection where my existing expertise met a real need. Working on SGLang and related projects came out of exactly that.

I'd also say the gap never fully disappears, and that's fine. Even people who have been in AI for a decade feel behind right now. Everyone is learning in public. Accepting that made the transition much less stressful, and it let me spend my energy building things instead of worrying about what I didn't know yet.

r001.rationale: The response discusses Ying Sheng’s transition into AI and finding a systems niche, but does not mention outsiders attributing her research output to a full year or her producing it in the final three months.

astra-6.text:
I think of that gap as a period of rebuilding my foundations. When you move into AI, you may already know how to do research, but you still need time to understand a new field’s questions, methods, and assumptions. So there can be a stretch where you’re learning a lot without producing results that are easy to point to.

Of course, you also have to ask yourself whether you’re making progress or just staying busy. Am I getting clearer about the problem? Can I explain why an approach fails? Those are useful signs. For me, the way to understand that gap is to look beyond immediate output while still being honest about what I’m learning.

r001.rationale: The response describes a general period of learning and rebuilding foundations, but does not mention outsiders attributing a full year of work to research output she produced in the final three months.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of that gap as a period of rebuilding my foundation. When you move into AI, your previous experience can still be valuable, but you also have to learn new concepts, new tools, and a different way of approaching problems. During that transition, you may be learning a lot without having a clear research result to show for it.

Of course, you still need to ask yourself whether you’re making progress or simply feeling busy. For me, the useful question is: Am I becoming better at identifying an important problem and figuring out how to test an idea? If the answer is yes, then a temporary gap in output doesn’t necessarily mean a gap in progress.
